question.text: Priya, a retail investor in Bengaluru, has 80% of her portfolio in IT stocks because she works in the IT sector and "understands technology well." She also believes her recent gains are due to her stock-picking skill. Which real-life deviations from rational behavior does Priya exhibit?

answer.text: Concentrated portfolio with sector/familiarity bias and attributing success to skill
Anchoring bias and status quo bias

explanation.text: The Logic: Real-life deviations from Standard Finance include concentrated portfolios instead of diversifying, sector concentration driven by familiarity/overconfidence, and attributing success to skill rather than market conditions. Priya shows both — overconfidence-driven sector concentration in IT (because she works in that sector) and self-attribution of recent gains to her own skill. The Trap: Loss aversion would apply if Priya were holding losing stocks to avoid realising losses. She is actually riding winners and crediting herself, which reflects overconfidence and sector/familiarity bias, not loss aversion. The workbook reserves "home bias" specifically for preference toward domestic securities, so labelling employer-sector preference as home bias would be inaccurate. Note: The workbook distinguishes overconfidence (causing portfolio concentration, excessive trading and sector bias) from home country bias (preference for domestic securities due to familiarity with the market, companies and regulation). Priya's case fits the former.
